I am actually suggesting a kind of general amnesty. I want to propose the following amendment as sub-paragraph 4 to Section 152:
(a)	Notwithstanding paragraph I52(4)(a), as of January 1, 1984, if any taxpayer or person Filing a return of income for taxation years prior to January 1, 1984, has made any misrepresentation in filing the return, the Minister shall not proceed with any reassessment, additional assessment or assessment of tax, interest or penalties under this Part.
(b)	Any proceedings relating to the reassessment, additional assessment or assessment of tax interest or penalties under this Part, on the basis that the taxpayer or person Filing a return of income has made any misrepresentation, and started and still pending before January 1, 1984, shall be dropped and no other proceedings undertaken for the taxation years ending before January I, 1984.
The general principle of this amendment is to prevent the Minister from issuing reassessments in cases of misrepresentation for the years prior to January 1, 1984. The amendment does not, of course, apply to taxpayers against whom court proceedings for tax recovery have already been initiated.
This is a constructive measure for economic renewal that will allow taxpayers to start with a clean slate. Mr. Speaker, 1 also feel that in future, we should consider a similar amendment to Section 239 of the same Act which concerns the possibility of bringing criminal charges against taxpayers who made false returns. A provision should be included to make it possible for any person anxious to set the record straight with Revenue Canada to file returns for the years prior to January 1, 1984 without fear of criminal or judicial proceedings.
Similarly, there has to be a limit on administrative penalties on returns for pre-1984 fiscal years.
Our opinion therefore is that all those measures will make our fellow Canadians regain confidence, forget about previous years and start anew without fearing that they might lose everything they had before 1984. In addition, these amendments are very much in keeping with the new government's ideology and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
December 11, 1984

Income Tax Act
In fact, the accused has the right to be tried within a reasonable time limit. It is very important that the taxpayer be deemed innocent, even in a case of infraction of the civil law.
Our proposed amendment to Section 239 closely reflects the spirit and feelings of the new government. Besides, the Progressive Conservative study group on the activities of Revenue Canada reached the same conclusion in April 1984: offenders have the right to be heard before being declared guilty. Let us not forget that most Canadians are honest citizens quite prepared to pay their taxes. They must have faith in our tax collectors rather than be afraid of them. The Minister has no time limit to review files in cases where fraud is suspected, otherwise it is four years after the first assessment notice. That certainly makes Canadians very insecure.
The same study group also pointed out that Revenue Canada was insensitive, discriminatory and disgraceful towards offenders, making them lose respect for the tax collection system which ought to have been fair and equitable. Let us be mindful of the fact that Canada's tax collection system rests on self-assessment and good will on the part of taxpayers who willingly file honest returns every year and pay any tax owing. Self-assessment has to be one of the most effective and least oppressing tax collection methods. The system will operate only as long as taxpayers support it. Their support will not be forthcoming unless they are convinced the system is fair and a climate of confidence prevails between both parties. Failing that, we breed mistrust, fear and deceit.
These amendments are designed to elicit voluntary divulgation of undeclared income by taxpayers who did not file a return, or filed one with mistakes or missing data. In one fell swoop, the State will fill its coffers by collecting-rather cheaply-taxes owing and recouping funds stashed away in foreign countries by delinquent taxpayers who are afraid to bring those funds back to Canada and draw the attention of Revenue Canada. This money could be laundered, brought back home and then invested to contribute to our economic recovery.
If the taxpayer has lost confidence in the fairness of our voluntary tax system, he will be tempted to join the so-called underground economy, which escapes taxation. By its very nature, the underground economy cannot be measured accurately, but its value is estimated to range between $40 and $80 billion. And although this is not sustained by any concrete evidence, we suspect that more and more money is being invested in this parallel economy. The greater part of this money is being exported to countries such as Switzerland and the Bahamas which are naturaly delighted to receive it. However, this money should stay in and benefit Canada, because huge amounts are involved. The delinquent taxpayer is not anxious to bring home his money for fear of incurring the wrath of Revenue Canada. As long as he feels this sword of Damocles hanging over his head, he will never try to bring his money back and invest it in this country. Thanks to these
amendments, we will be able to redirect toward the mainstream of our economy a good part of these funds. In an area of economic reconstruction, it is clearly advisable to patriate as much money as possible to serve the interest of the Canadian people as a whole.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that these amendements are a great step to help Canada make a new start.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the proposal made in the motion before the House is aimed at clearing up a very serious situation that has developed over the years. To our consternation, we found out recently that under the previous Government, there had been a rapid rise in income tax arrears. The so-called underground economy expanded as Canadians became involved in an increasing and alarming number of economic activities that were liable to escape the scrutiny of the tax collector. We believe that the total amount of unpaid taxes, that is, amounts owing to Revenue Canada which are not being contested, is now as high as $3.5 billion. This is a more than substantial amount since it represents over one-tenth of the federal deficit we inherited. In addition, there are also the taxes being avoided by the so-called underground economy. Unfortunately, we still have no accurate means of estimating the amount of income generated by the underground economy and undeclared economic activities that escape the scrutiny of Revenue Canada. There are, however, many indications that it is a very substantial amount that would be more than welcome in helping to reduce the federal deficit.
The proposal made by the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez) is in fact asking for an amnesty in cases where the taxpayer made an error or omission in filing his income tax return. I must say, with respect, that this proposal does raise a number of problems and some specific questions in my mind. First of all we must determine whether this is the best way to provide a fair solution to a rather complex problem. We should also ask ourselves what the consequences would be of such an amnesty. Giving an amnesty would be the same as saying that the problem no longer exists. It is certainly true that it would no longer exist for the taxpayers concerned. However, the problem would still exist for the Government which would have to give up hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue that could and should eventually be collected.
We must consider the situation in terms of the major objectives and priorities of the Government. In my opinion, there are three major objectives: bringing about an economic renewal in Canada, putting some order in public finance after many years of increasing deficits, and providing assistance to needy Canadians.
The proposal contained in the surprising motion now before us would go against these objectives. The proposed cancella-
December 11, 1984

tion of unpaid income taxes would increase the deficit and the Federal debt and in fact curtail the ability of the Government to contribute to economic renewal and growth. If this solution were applied, the Federal Treasury would be less capable of providing assistance to Canadians who really need it. This would be the direct and harmful impact such a proposal would have on the financial freedom of movement needed by our new Government to meet its objectives. In addition, this proposal would have major indirect effects of which the most important would be to alter our existing taxation system. This system at the present time is based on self-assessment by Canadian taxpayers. We trust Canadians to fairly report their own income and to submit the proper amount of tax. This system is based to a large extent on mutual trust and respect.
Indeed, the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Beatty) described this mechanism quite well in the unequivocal speech he gave before this Chambre last November 16 during the throne speech debate when he said the following:
For the self-assessment system to survive, all taxpayers must believe that they are being treated fairly and equally. At the same time, the Government must believe that all taxpayers will fairly report their income and submit the proper amount of tax on time.
If we were to agree to the proposal as it is worded in this motion, what would be the reaction of the majority of taxpayers who pay the proper amount of tax? Would they not be irritated by the increased burden placed on them because of the amnesty granted to others owing such a considerable amount of taxes? Would they not conclude that this type of amnesty favors those who have filed false tax returns in the past, whether accidentally or voluntarily? Would they not be tempted themselves in the future to file false statements in the hope that a convenient amnesty would eventually be granted in their own case?
I believe that the conclusion is clear. Such a procedure would greatly weaken our tax system. It would reward dishonesty while we are trying to encourage Canadian citizens to act honesty in their relations with the state. Instead of correcting the problem of unpaid taxes, this proposal would make it worse and it would degenerate uncontrollably. There is a definitely better solution, and this is the one followed by the Minister of National Revenue, who is implementing the conclusions and recommendations of the Progressive Conservative Task Force on Revenue Canada.
Let us consider the $3.5 million in back taxes which are not being questioned by taxpayers. This amount does not only represent the mistakes and omissions made in the past by taxpayers when filing their income tax returns. These are cases which the motion now before us attempts to deal with. This amount also includes taxes owed by taxpayers who have reported their full income but who are unable to pay their tax in full because they find themselves in a temporary financial bind.
Income Tax Act
The Minister of National Revenue has indicated that there was a distinction to be drawn between taxpayers who try to evade tax and those who because of financial difficulties cannot pay, at least momentarily.
The Minister of National Revenue is committed to a humane, compassionate and tactful treatment by Revenue Canada of people in need. Past experience unfortunately has shown that a stringent attitude by Revenue Canada could generate distrust, noncompliance, frustration and even bitterness. It is possible and it is important to be both firm and fair. Revenue Canada has finally taken a number of definite steps to increase the efficiency of the tax collecting process. The Department will hire additional staff, and this will enable collectors to spend more time with deserving taxpayers who momentarily find it difficult to pay their taxes. Mutually acceptable arrangements will provide for the staggering of payments. The Department's set target is to collect $400 million over and above the unpaid moneys that normally would be collected by Revenue Canada under the former procedure.
The Minister has also pondered over the problems of Canadians who fail to report income earned from so-called underground practices and activities. In his explicit address to the Canadian Association of Tax Studies, he urged taxpayers who had failed to report all their income to come forward and pay their taxes, without fear of legal action, under the new departmental regulations dealing with voluntary returns. This is but one of a number of reforms designed to give Revenue Canada a more humane, more efficient and less stringent profile.
In the area of collection, in-service training programs for tax collectors will be implemented so that the collecting of unpaid taxes will become a better and more accurate process. Where taxes are due, Revenue Canada will send out a series of notices of collection that will set out more clearly the Department's relevant policy and the rights of the taxpayers. Then, before finally taking legal action, the tax collectors will be required to try to the best of their ability to contact, by telephone or otherwise, the defaulting taxpayers and give him every possible chance to pay his debt, without having to resort to the cumbersome intricacies of legal proceedings.
Hon. Members of this dignified House will know surely that the amendments to the Income Tax Act now before the House include a number of measures advocating a legislation reform.
One of the basic causes of taxpayer resentment in the past has been the feeling that, whenever assessments are opposed, the taxpayer is considered guilty until proven otherwise. Such a position, contrary to our basic judicial system, was held because in the past taxpayers were required to pay the full amount of the objectionable assessments even before the dispute had been resolved or even examined.

December 11, 1984
Income Tax Act
The new legislation provides that the taxpayer will not have to pay the disputed tax until the matter has indeed been heard. In order to prevent the new system from being abused, the courts will be empowered to impose penalties for irresponsible appeals.
Other amendments to the Income Tax Act are actually aiming for the same goal, namely handling taxpayers with fairness, sensivity and respect. The Canadian Tax Court therefore has the power to refund appeal costs to taxpayers, so that they will not abstain from appealing a decision before a neutral, fair and impartial court for mere financial reasons. Also, the maximum period for the Department to establish new assessments has been reduced from four to three years in all cases except willful evasion, blatant negligence or obvious fraud.
Those are some of the proposals for positive changes to the Act. A number of other amendments of a technical nature that already have been or are in the process of being introduced also are aimed, as I have already said, at treating taxpayers in a fairer, more humane way.
There was a time when the Minister of National Revenue had a quota system. This method of assessing the work done by tax auditors must be dropped because they often saw it as an incentive do be unduly harsh with taxpayers. In other words, the new system will stress quality rather than quantity. Another practice which has been stopped is the premature enlightenment of the medias every time a taxpayer is accused-even before the trial-and the reprehensible habit of releasing the names of people mentioned in regular reports on inquiries conducted by the department.
A few days ago, the Minister of National Revenue announced a series of improvements to the tax administration system. For instance, when a Revenue Canada auditor checks a tax return, he will get in touch more often with the taxpayer before changing the amount of tax owing, and the taxpayer will have more time to prepare his response, 30 days instead of 21 days, as is the case now. Anyway, the 30-day delay is a common practice in business circles. Written explanations concerning new computerized assessments will provide more details and data in clearer and less ambiguous terms. That will certainly help taxpayers know exactly where they stand.
Communication services between taxpayers and Revenue Canada are being modernized, a definite plus at the critical tax-return time when the Canadian taxpayer is most in need of information, clarifications and even advice. The network of tax assistance seasonal centres will be enlarged and 24 new such centres will be opened. Business hours for free telephone services offered by district offices will be extended during the busy period when most tax returns are usually filed. Special communication services will soon be available for people who suffer from blindness or hearing difficulties.
Is this not an impressive although incomplete list of the changes which Revenue Canada intends to make where its
relations with the Canadian public are concerned? These progressive initiatives are the follow up of the major conclusions reached earlier this year by the Progressive Conservative Task Force, which found that the unbending attitude too often present in the past simply frustrated taxpayers and caused them to resist and to avoid paying taxes. This fresh new attitude illustrates the firm conviction of this Government that Canadians can be trusted.
I believe that, after due consideration to the proposal made by the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez), we should feel this same confidence in Canadian taxpayers and not presume that Canadians generally will refuse to pay their tax. In the past, these taxpayers may have had valid reasons not to trust the former Government and to conclude that they had nothing to do with its financial problems. In this case, the simplistic solution of declaring an amnesty for fed-up taxpayers is definitely unacceptable. The real answer lies in providing taxpayers with every opportunity to settle their accounts and, in cases of financial difficulties, to wait for their situation to improve.
The second element of this solution which heralds a new era is to improve Government operations. In this way taxpayers will have fewer valid reasons in the future to have problems and to resent a Government which used to be arrogant. I truly believe that the progressive and positive reforms we intend to bring about in the operations of Revenue Canada are a perfect example of the type of renewal in public administration which responsible Canadians are looking forward. Thank you, Mr. Speaker.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Member for Regina East (Mr. de Jong).
Hear, hear!

I thank the Hon. Members for the applause. Mr. Speaker, I wish to join in the debate on the Private Member's Bill introduced by the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez). I am afraid the Hon. Member for Chateauguay failed to convince me and I would venture to say he failed to convince most Members of this House of the justification for his Private Member's Bill. As the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Revenue and Canada Post (Mr. Vincent) has pointed out, this Private Member's Bill would give in essence an amnesty to all taxpayers who might have deliberately or not deliberately falsified their tax returns in the previous year. Certainly we do not believe that this is how the problem that faces the Canadian Government and the taxpayers should be solved.
I am afraid the Parliamentary Secretary and the Minister himself are somewhat naive when they believe that an honest appeal by this Government would automatically mean that hundreds of thousands of people, corporations, businesses large
December 11, 1984

and small, which in the past might have cheated a little on their tax would all at once come forward and do the right thing. In this new era which the Government claims it has established, would truth and justice like a bolt of lightning hit all taxpayers and from now on we will have nothing but honesty prevailing in this field? I feel the Minister and the Parliamentary Secretary are somewhat naive. I hope this is just propaganda and really not government policy. If this is government policy, we will be in some difficulty in the years ahead.
Paying taxes in an exercise that most people the world over do not relish. People feel that these are moneys they have earned either through business activity or labour. They want to keep as much of that money for their own use. Of course, in a society like ours that is dependent very much upon government activity to maintain our roads to provide health services and to do all the things a modern state must do in order for a modern civilization to exist, one of the forms of revenue for these purposes must be the tax system.
The tax system must be fair and must appear to be fair. It must appear and in reality be something whereby people are treated on an equal basis. In our system and in the system of most of the industrialized civilized world there is a progressive income tax system. The greater your income, the greater your ability to help foot the public bill, and according to our system, the greater amount you are called upon to contribute to the national purpose. Again, it should be realized that most people who earn an income do so with the assistance of government in one form or another. If we did not have our health system, our education system, our rail and road system, and what not, most Canadians could not earn an income. The ability to earn that income is dependent upon the fact that we have a modern state providing these essential services.
For the Hon. Member to suggest in his Private Member's Bill that the Department of National Revenue should be restricted to auditing returns only for this year, and that the taxpayer be given an amnesty so that the Department would no longer be able to audit returns for 1984 and prior, I do not think it will help the Government or make the tax system fairer.
When you look at Revenue Canada taxation estimates, for 1984-85, Mr. Speaker, you see two important activities that the Department carries on. One is post assessing. This operation consists of the examination of certain things for deduction or exemption which are accepted without question at the initial assessing in order to expedite the flow of returns. In other words, when the income tax returns come in, the National Revenue Department gives them a very brief look. Most of the forms are accepted at face value. Taxes are collected. Cheques are issued for money owed to a taxpayer, and so forth. Subsequently, I understand about 3 per cent of the returns are audited. As well, the Department audits to make sure income reported on the tax form is the income supported by such slips as T-4s from employers and the T-5s from the banks.
We find in the Estimates for 1984-85 that this activity in the year 1982-83 brought in some $828,948,000, which is a
Income Tax Act
fair chunk of change so to speak. In essence, what this Private Member's Bill is suggesting is that the Government forgo these revenues. Remember that this figure of $828 million which the Government collected because of its audit functions really covered only 3 per cent of corporations that filed income tax returns. This means that a fair amount of money is not collected. It means that a fair number of companies, either deliberately or not deliberately, fill out their corporate tax sheets in an improper way. All of the information is not there. It means that a 3 per cent audit netted the Government, just on the corporation side, some $645 million last year. What the Private Member's Bill suggests is that the Government kisses $645 million good-bye. If we had tremendous surpluses in government revenues perhaps there would be some justification for this. I wish the Hon. Member would express his indignation at the $200 million which the Government wants to save by cutting back on unemployment insurance.
The Hon. Member, I am sure, will be supportive of the Government's cut-backs to the UIC program. I am sure there are people ripping the system off. May I suggest that those people are people with very low incomes? Yet the Government is willing to hire several hundred policemen to police UIC recipients. I am sure they will be given quotas and they will be forced to justify their income by making sure that a certain percentage of the people they interview every day will be found ineligible for UIC payments.
The Government should be as concerned about collecting the $3.5 billion which is owed to it. These moneys are not in dispute. Heaven knows the amount of money owed to the Government which is in dispute. However, there is this $3.5 billion which everyone agrees is owed to the Government. It is out there. It is 10 per cent of the deficit.
Day in and day out we stand in the House to try to imprint upon the Government that it does not have a deficit because of overspending. The deficit is there because the Government has not been collecting the taxes it should be collecting. The deficit could be reduced off the top by 10 per cent if the Government would only collect the undisputed amount of money due to it.
The area of undisputed tax which galls me the most is the $328 million or so which employers have deducted from their employees. These deductions were in the form of income tax, UIC and CCP. These moneys have not been remitted to the Government. They are held in trust. It is not even their money. It used to be some $428 million, but the Minister has already kissed $100 million off. He said that he would not bother collecting that, that it was dead, that it was gone. There is still some $328 million owing to the public Treasury by people who hold this money in trust.
I understand that such workers are eligible for UIC payments if the corporation goes bankrupt and still owes the Government money from UIC deductions. I also understand that very often these workers experience tremendous difficulty in obtaining the coverage owing to them. It is a long, drawn-out fight to gain the coverage for which they have paid. For

December 11, 1984
Income Tax Act
the Hon. Member to suggest in his Bill that there ought to be an amnesty I find a little too much. In fact, it contradicts his own Party's task force on Revenue Canada. In its report the following was indicated:
The Task Force sympathizes with these taxpayers yet recognizes that the Minister must have adequate time in which to audit tax returns. However, it also believes that four years is excessive and suggests a three year time frame, when fraud is not involved.
We will have to see the type of legislation the Minister will be introducing to limit the period of time within which audits occur. I hope the Government is sincere in reducing its deficit and in ensuring that we have a fair taxation system. All Canadians should be treated equally and fairly. I am hoping that we do not have one tax law for the rich and another for the poor. I am hoping that we do not have one tax law for big corporations which are able to hire tax accountants and tax lawyers to keep the Government spinning in circles and another tax law for the small ones. These large corporations can hold on to hundreds of millions of dollars in unpaid taxes. They can use these moneys internally and save a fair amount because the penalty charged by the Government is prime minus one. It is in the interests of these corporations to retain these hundreds of millions of dollars within the corporate sector because the amount of interest they are paying is much less than they would have to pay at the bank. I hope the Government is as anxious to go after the big guys as it is to go after the small guys. I hope everyone is indeed treated equally and fairly. We have some distance to go in this regard.
Let us look at what a salaried worker pays in income tax, the number of his deductions and the number of income tax games he can play compared with corporations. We see that fairness does not exist. There is no way a salaried worker can hide income. He does not have similar exemptions. For example, he cannot defer taxes. However, there are some $32 billion in deferred taxes owed to the Government of Canada. That is enough to wipe out the deficit. Although salaried workers are unable to defer taxes, corporations seem to enjoy that benefit.
I understand CPR owes some $1.5 billion in deferred taxes.
Hear, hear!

I hear the Hon. Member for Crowfoot (Mr. Malone) saying "Hear, hear". He is another fan of the CPR. I am sure there are many more across the way. This is why I do not have much faith in the Government opposite that we will have a fair taxation regime and that everyone will be treated equally. The CPR should be treated in the same way as the people working for it and drawing salaries. I doubt the banks will end up paying the same amount of tax that all their clerks pay. Indeed I doubt that we will have a fair taxation system with the people who are able to afford it paying their fair share. We do not have a fair taxation system. We really do not have a progressive system. In fact, it is the inverse. The people least able to pay, average working men and women, pay the most. The people best able to pay are the ones who pay the least. The economic philosophy and policies of the Government encourage that even further. I really do not expect a fair taxation policy from the Government. We will see. We will
attempt to push the Government into accepting a basic fairness in our taxation regime.
I find the Private Member's Bill of the Hon. Member for Chateauguay to be unacceptable. I expect that it is unacceptable to the Hon. Member for Crowfoot. I am sure it will be unacceptable to most Members on the government side. It makes an unfair system more unfair and therefore repugnant to Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, without wishing to take up too much of the House's time, I simply want to say that if there is a vote, we shall be voting against the present proposal. I do feel rather sorry for the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez), since he is not getting much support from his own colleagues for a proposal into which he probably put a lot of work.
I also think it is rather ironic that basically, the Hon. Member for Chaateauguay is only putting into practice what his hon. colleagues said they would do when they criss-crossed the country on their partisan committee to seek the views of Canadian taxpayers on our tax system. The message they gave at the time and to which his own colleagues might well object today, was that there was so much abuse on the part of the Department of National Revenue, and so it seemed quite normal to the Hon. Member and in line with the Progressive Conservative policy over the last two years, to present this proposal and try to eliminate in one fell swoop all those flagrant examples of injustice.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Chateauguay will learn, as will Canadian taxpayers, that there is a considerable gap between the rhetoric of his Party's politicians and what they actually do here in the House. I feel very sorry for him, and I hope he will get some sympathy from his colleagues and will get them to understand that when a message is given to Canadians, it must be considered when the time comes to pass legislation.
And now, Mr. Speaker, I think I may say, in more general terms, that it is clear the Government of a country cannot afford to let an amendment consisting of three or four lines deprive it of all the money owed by some taxpayers just because there might have been some omission or error in their income tax returns. It would be too easy for people to avoid paying what they owe, to avoid paying their fair share to finance public expenditures, and all for reasons that are basically futile. It would also be unfair to taxpayers who are not in arrears, who file complete returns and who meet their obligations as responsible citizens by paying their taxes.
I heard the Hon. Member for LaSalle (Mr. Lanthier) make some suggestions. Mr. Speaker, if there is a way to humanize the Income Tax Act, whether we are referring to the federal, provincial or municipal provisions in this respect, obviously no
December 11, 1984

one can object to that. However, the fact remains that the only way to collect money is to get people to pay.
I feel that the message we are getting from our friends opposite, or at least the message they may be getting through to Canadian taxpayers, is that now the Progressive Conservative Party is in power, there are going to be lots of ways to avoid paying taxes. There are going to be plenty of opportunities for the reason who owes $100,000 or $200,000 in taxes, when the interest rate paid by the bank is higher than the fine a judge might impose, as the Member for LaSalle said. There will be a lot of people, a lot of taxpayers who will be tempted to use the tax office as a bank instead of getting their own financing and paying the taxes they do owe the Government, in any case.
I think that what the Hon. Member for LaSalle is saying- and a few days ago, I heard the Minister of National Revenue speaking in the same vein, and the House will recall most of the speeches made during the election campaign-is that it is doing Canadians a disservice to give the impression that there are many ways of avoiding taxes and putting off paying them, and finally, that this would penalize the honest taxpayer who pays his taxes on time. I think this is not the impression a responsible Government ought to give, unless sooner or later it is prepared to accept proposals like the one made by the Member for Chateauguay. If that is the case, I would urge the Hon. Member for Chateauguay to go around the House and persuade his colleagues to vote for him, because his proposal is in line with the impression this Government wanted to give earlier.
Mr. Speaker, I will not use up any more of the House's time. If it even comes to a vote on this motion, we shall certainly vote against it.

Mr. Speaker, I understand quite well the concern which my colleague the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Garneau) has expressed; he knows how difficult it is to collect money, in view of his occupation before his election to the House. I must say, however, that the motion moved by our colleague is one which we should consider and discuss seriously.
Until six o'clock.

Perhaps until six o'clock, I agree, Mr. Speaker; what we must take into account, however, is its impact on the Canadian public as a whole.
Clearly, there are some people who, over the years, have been lucky enough-if I can use that expression-not to pay any income tax, but that does not necessarily mean that we should set a rule and apply it unilaterally to all Canadians, as the previous administration used to do.
I shall not delay the House any longer, Mr. Speaker. I simply wanted to indicate that the motion moved by my
Income Tax Act
colleague the Hon. Member for Chateauguay is fine per se, but I wonder whether it was sensible to introduce it today.

Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Chateauguay (Mr. Lopez) knows full well that his motion touches on a branch of the law which concerned the Progressive Conservative Party well in advance of the September 4 election to a very great degree, to the degree that at our own expense this Party formed a task force that travelled across the land to identify the attitude and problems and the specific concerns that affected the taxpayers of this land.
Many of those concerns were reflected in the votes that were cast on September 4, returning a Party which had a concern for the taxpayer in heart and in mind. That task force came up with a report entitled "A Taxayers Bill of Rights". During that election campaign, our Party made a commitment that this Government would be responsive to the needs and concerns of the individual taxpayer. Nowhere is this more important than in the dealings between Government and citizen as it is in the administration of our tax laws. The aims of the Government were spelled out in great detail in the Speech from the Throne opening this new session. It stated:
The taxation system will be made simpler and fairer and more accountable to the people's representatives in Parliament. The rights of taxpayers must be protected. In particular, legislation will be presented to ensure that no taxpayer has to pay taxes in dispute before an impartial hearing has been concluded.
As an additional protection, taxpayers launching future objections will be eligible to file claims for the refund of disputed amounts already paid and these will be returned if the case is not dealt with expeditiously by the Department within a reasonable period of time. There will be protection against abuse of these new privileges in that the courts will be empowered to assess penalties where it is clear that taxpayers have launched frivolous or groundless appeals purely to delay the payment of taxes legally owed.
One of the most significant of the changes made is to exempt persons with taxes payable of $1,000 or less from the requirement to pay in quarterly instalments. In the past, quarterly payments have been required for those with taxes of $400 or more. The main beneficiaries will be 350,000 senior citizens who will be freed of the obligation to make their tax payments in instalments. This new threshold of $1,000 will also apply to corporations. It will be of great assistance to some 50,000 corporations, mainly small businesses and family farm corporations.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-WORK OF REVIEW COMMITTEE. (B) COMPOSITION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-WORK OF REVIEW COMMITTEE. (B) COMPOSITION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the day after the new Cabinet was sworn in, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced that the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Nielsen), along with the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), the Minister of Justice (Mr. Crosbie) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) had been assigned the task of reviewing all departmental programs and submitting action plans for Cabinet approval within six months. This was generally considered to be a way of prescribing more cuts. That has not been denied.
Subsequently, an advisory committee of seven businessmen was named. This committee did not include any women, Francophones, environmentalists, representatives from health and social services or from consumers' associations. Two names of union officials were included but then subsequent reports cast doubts upon whether or not they would in fact be participating or what the nature of their participation would be.
At a press conference on November 18, the President of the Treasury Board said that neither the Treasury Board Secretariat nor the office of the Comptroller General had been targeted for review. "We don't take programs," were the words attributed to the President of the Treasury Board.
In terms of numbers, there are between 50,000 and 60,000 person-years involved in programs of the central agencies as compared with perhaps 170,000 or more involved in delivering services to taxpayers. If cuts are necessary, surely they should be done with great care, delicacy and sensitivity and done equally in all Departments.
This is the kind of thing that raises the question of whether cuts are being taken on the basis of ideology or on the basis of efficiency. We hear a lot of talk about how the Government means to cut fat out of the bureaucracy but we are really talking about people and their jobs and about people delivering services to other people.
A few days ago, I asked the Deputy Prime Minister if he would confirm that the central agencies were being excluded from the cuts. He answered that the premise of my question was wrong and that he was not involved in a cutting exercise but in an exercise of looking at duplications, overlaps and so on and that all Departments would be treated equally. I then asked the Deputy Prime Minister if he would restructure his advisory committee to reflect this kind of mandate. I cannot see that an advisory committee composed of only seven businessmen who have purely administrative backgrounds is competent alone without other assistance to advise on eliminating programs to do with the environment, health, social services and so on.
The Deputy Prime Minister gave me a very broad and general answer which described what appeared to be consultations with the Quebec Federation of Labour but he did not say exactly if or how he intends to alter his advisory committee. I am pleased to see the Deputy Prime Minister in the House this evening and I look forward to receiving more precise information.

speakeroldname: Hon. Erik Nielsen (Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: GOVERNMENT EXPENDITURES-WORK OF REVIEW COMMITTEE. (B) COMPOSITION OF ADVISORY COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad the Hon. Member gave me this opportunity to clarify what the Task Force on Program Review was all about. I think it is important that she and other Members of the House are as well informed as possible regarding an exercise which is not targeted at cost cutting at all, but is targeted at improving efficiency and delivery to the client groups outside of the internal structure of Government and to looking inside as well.
The terms of reference of the task force were announced on September 18 when the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) announced the creation of the task force and its composition under my chairmanship. We have been asked to review government programs with the intent to produce a profile of government programs which is simpler, more understandable and more accessible to the Canadian public, to their clientele, and where decision-making is decentralized as far as possible with those in direct contact with client groups.
The task force itself has been asked and mandated to begin reporting within six months, the termination date being March 17. The work program, in order to address its task with a sense of order and intelligence, has set its objective to compile an inventory of all of those programs in Government, which has been accomplished. The second stage was to deal with those broad program categories.
With respect to the advisory committee, I can tell the Hon. Member that the task force Ministers made a very deliberate decision to involve the private sector in a very positive and meaningful way. To do this we have called upon national organizations-which was part of my announcement on November 16-with respect to the creation of a Private Sector Advisory Committee. This Committee is now, at this moment-which is some time from when the Hon. Member asked her question-made up of representatives of the Canadian Federation of Labour, represented by Mr. Austin Thorne; the Canadian Labour Congress, represented by Mr. Robert Baldwin; the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants, represented by Mr. Phillip Aspinall, who has been elected Chairman by the choice of the private sector advisory committee; the Business Council on National Issues, represented by Mr. Jerry Heffernan; and the Canadian Association of Management Consultants, represented by Mr. Ted Netten. All of these individuals were designated by those organizations them-

selves. There is the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, represented by Mr. Peter Riggin; the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, represented by Mr. Harold Milavsky; the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, represented by Mr. Ronald Farano; the Canadian Organization of Small Business, represented by Mr. Geoffrey Hale; Conseil du Patronat du Quebec, represented by Jean D'Ailly, whose name, I am sure, will be familiar to the Hon. Member; le Groupement Quebecois d'entreprises, represented by Mr. Richard Bourbeau. Mr. Laberge of the Quebec Federation of Labour, who was supposed to get back to me today, has not done so, but I am sure that I will hear from him before the week is out. It is an ongoing process. In addition, Mr. Darcy McKeough, the former Treasurer of Ontario, has been appointed as Private Sector Liaison adviser in order to provide liaison between myself, in my capacity as Chairman of the Task Force, and the Private Sector Advisory Committee.
I believe that all Hon. Members of the House will want to join with me in tendering our gratitude and congratulations to these designated individuals for serving on a Private Sector Advisory Committee involving this very important work at a dollar a year. With no cost to the taxpayer whatsoever, we are involving the private sector in a very meaningful and productive way in this task of program review.
On the public side, our activities involve our appointment of Dr. Peter Meyboom as the Public Service Adviser to co-ordinate whatever studies are necessary during the assessment phase of our work. To date, as I announced on November 19, the program inventory is now complete. It contains 989 programs delivering a total of $92 billion in direct and indirect benefits to individuals, businesses, organizations or a combination of all three. A total of 126 Departments and agencies are responsible for the delivery of these programs, involving 173,000 person years.
I invite the Hon. Member, and all Hon. Members of the House, to co-operate with us in this work to streamline and make more effective and efficient the delivery of these programs to the public, and to examine those internal programs as well, which is going to result in more efficiency and effectiveness by Government.

subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-CANADIAN WILDLIFE SERVICE-CANCELLATION OF HERRING GULL EGG PROGRAM. (B) MINISTER'S VIEW
ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-CANADIAN WILDLIFE SERVICE-CANCELLATION OF HERRING GULL EGG PROGRAM. (B) MINISTER'S VIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to pursue a question I asked of the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier) with respect to cutbacks in her Department. In doing so, I would like to express my concern on three fronts, if you will.
We have before us in the form of various cuts initiated by this Government a package which is cause for despair among those of us concerned about the environment, in that we seem to be moving towards rather than back from the day when we will have an economy and society based on the proper stewardship and management of our resources and our common
Adjournment Debate
planetary heritage. The three areas I refer to are cutbacks in the research program of the Canadian Wildlife Service, the cut of the NRC environmental secretariat, and the cutbacks in research and development in the area of alternate energy.
First of all, Mr. Speaker, with respect to that which has received the most attention, the cutbacks in the research program of the Canadian Wildlife Service, I would just like to put on the record some of the things which have been cut. We have the Wildlife toxicology projects which go under the following names. The identification and monitoring of the occurrence and effects of toxic substances on gulls and other fish-eating birds on the Great Lakes. That is a very important program and part of Canada's contribution to the Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement. There is the monitoring of effects of forestry insecticides on birds in New Brunswick, the monitoring of effects of agricultural rodenticides and insecticides on birds in Alberta, identifying effects of toxic substances on bird populations in the Great Lakes, and the monitoring of contaminants in birds on the Fraser River Delta in British Columbia. Then there are projects to rehabilitate endangered species which have been cancelled; the reintroduction of Peregrine Falcons in eastern Canada, in Nova Scotia, the rehabilitation of the Piping Plover in the Maritimes, and the reintroduction of the Pine Marten to Newfoundland. In this same area veterinary pathology services, and bioelectronic services have been cancelled. Programs in conservation of international wildlife, like the Porcupine Caribou program, which I have mentioned in this House before, have been cancelled. There are interprovincial and territorial agreements which have been affected, such as the CWS membership on the Beverly-Kaminuriak Caribou Management Board. There is the whole matter of support to other federal services which has been cut in forestry, national parks and other federal lands. And then there is wildlife interpretation where there have been severe cuts. Then, Mr. Speaker, we have the cuts, as I mentioned, in the NRC environmental secretariat, a body which has produced between 80 and 90 reports on subjects such as acid rain, herbicides, insecticides, fluorides, PCBs, mercury, lead and noise pollution in the past 15 years. It is an impartial source of scientific information on which governments have been able to base their decisions. It is a disaster that this kind of research is being cut out by the Government.
The third dimension of my concern, Mr. Speaker, and I have raised this in the House with the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney), is in relation to the cuts in alternative energy research and development, and how they compare to the absolutely uncritical approach of the Government to the furtherance of the nuclear energy option in Canada.
As a result of recent Government cuts, we have a 100 per cent cut in conservation and alternative energy research and development. That contrasts with trends elsewhere in the world. There is a trend to Government support for R and D in this area in the U.S., West Germany and Japan. That trend is not recognized by the Conservatives. In the United States alone they will spend $174.5 million in direct support while

December 11, 1984
Adjournment Debate
millions more is raised through R and D limited partnerships. Instead of that, from this Government we get cuts in the work of the NRC in active solar research. The NRC provided an essential base for product improvement and price reduction, reducing the price of a standard solar domestic hot water package from $4,000 in 1982 to $2,700 in 1984. The NRC was on schedule to bring the cost to $1,500 by 1988, at which time solar would be competitive across Canada with conventional sources of energy.
Before the cut-backs in conservation and alternative energy research and development, over 60 per cent of the Government's funding in energy R and D went into the nuclear area. That percentage will now be much higher, Mr. Speaker. I suppose the Tory reason for this is that they cannot figure out a way to put a meter on the sun. If you cannot make money off it, it cannot be worthwhile. We know that if the Tories do figure out a way to put a meter on the sun and sell the franchise to a multinational, then we might get solar research.
The Minister has said that a higher principle was involved. That higher principle was the cutting of the deficit. Mr. Speaker, there is no higher principle than the preservation of human life and our common planetary heritage in which that life must carry on. The Government is fond of talking about the deficit, and mortgaging our future. By engaging in the kinds of cut-backs in environmental services that it is now engaged in, it is mortgaging our environmental future. That is the kind of mortgaging of our future that cannot be paid back in the same way that a financial deficit can be. Until the Government realizes that, it will continue to lead us down the road to ecological disaster.

speakeroldname: Hon. Suzanne Blais-Grenier (Minister of the Environment):
subtopic: ENVIRONMENTAL AFFAIRS-CANADIAN WILDLIFE SERVICE-CANCELLATION OF HERRING GULL EGG PROGRAM. (B) MINISTER'S VIEW
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful to my colleague for this highly emotional intervention which gives me the opportunity to provide more information on cutbacks in my department and tell Canadians that my colleague of the Opposition is indulging in pure and simple demagoguery.
As I said before in the House, my department, in cooperation with the Department of National Health and Welfare and the Department of Oceans and Fisheries, is pursuing research on toxic products and monitoring their effects, particularly in the Great Lakes area. Environment Canada now has 78 highly qualified employees in that region.
Mr. Speaker, the cutbacks amount to 305 person-years in a department with over 10,000 employees. As I said time and again, I have always been prepared to reconsider, if necessary, those cutbacks which have to do with our federal responsibilities or international agreements, or which might possibly affect the health of Canadians. I did say I would have consultations.
I spoke with many scientists, people active in the programs involved and some of our representatives within international research or monitoring agencies. The Herring Gull Egg Program has come under close scrutiny, due consideration being given to other resources in the department. I came to the conclusion that we can maintain the egg monitoring program by meshing it with the activities of Burlington's Wastewater Technology Centre.
I told the Canadian co-chairman of the Great Lakes Joint Monitoring Commission about this decision, and he gave me the assurance that it did not in any way detract from our international commitments.
I might also remind my colleague that toxicological research is going on in 24 departments, as prescribed in 58 acts or regulations, and that our efforts aimed at improving Canadian expertise in that field are being maintained and increased.
I want to reassure Canadians, Mr. Speaker. We are aware of our responsibilities. We assume them. We do not shirk them.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-ESCAPE OF THREE INMATES FROM BATH INSTITUTION
PENITENTIARIES-ESCAPE OF THREE INMATES FROM BATH INSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am grateful for this opportunity to speak further on a matter of great concern that I raised on December 5, 1984 in the House. At that time I directed a question to the Solicitor General (Mr. MacKay) regarding a recent escape from the Bath Institution and hostage-taking incident at Bath, Ontario. This incident greatly disturbs me.
Three inmates broke out of the Bath Institution and forcibly entered a private residence. A retired couple from Bath were aroused from their sleep, tied up with a clothes line and held at gunpoint. They watched helplessly as the inmates searched their home for money, broke into a gun cabinet and stole three weapons. The inmates then fled in the family car.
People should not have to take the time or bear the expense to bring these convicts before the courts once again. I hope that the Solicitor General will impress upon his officials that it is the primary duty of Correctional Services Canada to ensure custody and control of inmates in order to minimize the risk of harm being inflicted by inmates on the public, the staff, other inmates or themselves. At the same time, of course, we should recognize international standards of human treatment.
If inmates continue to escape, our correctional system will no longer be serving the people by protecting society from these criminals; those people who have demonstrated by their actions that they cannot and will not live by the commonsense and common decency of our society. Victims of crime are quite often forced to pay in real terms for having been at a certain place at the wrong time. I am also advised that the OPP are often called to retrieve inmates from various public places. Apparently, it is a common event for prisoners to walk to the village in order to have a few alcoholic drinks.
December 11, 1984

There are three specific points that I would like to urge on all Members of the Elouse, specifically on the Minister, for their evaluation. First, the process involved in the classification of prisoners must be closely examined. Perhaps the principle should be altered to more accurately reflect the goal of protecting our society; not just for the protection of the individual who is incarcerated. Somehow, this has been twisted around. We are putting criminals into institutions from which the inmates can escape and go for a drink or a joy ride. This must stop. The process of classifying prisoners is in serious need of revision. We must ensure that the punishment fits the crime, not the criminals' own needs.
Another point I wish to make concerns the deterrent concept of our criminal system. There are two concepts in this area; rehabilitation and retribution. Rehabilitation implies that the purpose behind imprisoning people who have contravened the law is to rehabilitate them so that they can return to our society as someone new, ready and willing to participate in our society. This may be a noble concept but I have serious doubts as to its effectiveness. In most cases the rehabilitation concept removes the responsibility of the crime from the criminal. This is not right. Our society is based on our citizens being responsible for their actions. 1 am not denying that some people need help and should receive it, but I believe we have gone overboard in some cases. In our attempt to help a few we have removed the principle of being responsible for one's own actions.
The concept of retribution is the other point. Retribution means atonement or satisfaction given for injury. In order to make our correctional and judicial system work we cannot forget the value of retribution. If we do, we will fail in our attempt to provide a fair, just and appropriate correctional system. I urge the Minister to seriously examine the purpose and intent of our correctional system. If we take away the responsibility for one's action, how can that person ever return to a society in which we are responsible for our actions? Serving time for crimes against society is not enough. That is why I believe our correctional system must have punishment to fit the crime. It is hard to determine a just punishment for persons who induce terror by holding people at gunpoint. Sending two potted plants and some money may be very fine, but it is not retribution, especially when it is not from the people who are directly involved.
My third point concerns the security of our correctional institutions. When I hear of a prison escape and the terrible events that sometimes follow, such as in the recent Bath Institution case, I become very alarmed. How can we allow people who are being held accountable for some crime already committed to commit yet another crime? In order to ensure that retribution is paid for crimes already committed, we have a responsibility to the victim of the crime, society and even the criminal that the security and enforcement of the punishment is complete and not lacking anything. The people charged with securing and ensuring that the sentence be carried out must be given the resources and money to do so. That means everything from perimeter control to the authority necessary to
Adjournment Debate
maintain an institution at the local level. I urge the Minister to ensure that these resources are provided to the correctional systems' employees. The employees need our support.
Finally, may I add that the recent incident concerning the Bath Institution is not the only situation about which I am concerned. It is an example of the terrible things that are being allowed to happen. These must stop. I ask the Solicitor General to give this House and all Canadians his assurance that such matters as prisoner classification, appropriate punishment, and improvement of security in our correctional institutions will be dealt with quickly and carefully. These are matters of extreme importance.

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer M. MacKay (Solicitor General of Canada);
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-ESCAPE OF THREE INMATES FROM BATH INSTITUTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to respond this evening and put on the record the appreciation I have for my colleague for bringing this serious matter to the attention of the House. 1 want to thank him for the meeting we had in the recent past when he brought some of these concerns to my attention in another forum.
The Hon. Member raised this question the day after it occurred in a conscientious and timely manner. As he has pointed out, there have been some developments in the interim. The three men involved were arrested the next day, December 5, and are now in custody. In a rare show of concern, and 1 think in an appropriate one, although as he pointed out, it did not involve the escapees themselves, the other inmates at Bath Institution took up a collection, collected a significant amount of money for needy people in the area and sent an apology and some flowers to the elderly couple their former comrades had victimized in that escape.
As the Hon. Member knows, Bath Institution is a minimum security institution. While it has no perimeter fence or outside patrol, security precautions are taken. There are counts of inmates every 45 minutes. There are other checks and there are alarmed doors.
In order to be placed in such a minimum security facility an inmate must show by his behaviour that he is a suitable candidate. Prediction of suitability or prediction of human behaviour is an inexact science at best. I believe our people in the department have done a reasonably good job, but that is not to say there is not room for improvement. We look at factors such as the length of sentence, the type of crime, the history of violence in the community and the risk of escape.
These three inmates were all serving their first federal terms. They all started their terms in medium security institutions and their behaviour up to that point was satisfactory. While they were at Bath no problems were observed. In fact, two of these men had successfully completed unescorted temporary absences. One of the three, however, had earlier this year been unlawfully at large from another minimum security institution. I am concerned about this and 1 will pass my concerns on to the Commissioner. This inmate did not by his behaviour demonstrate an undue risk. One of the three was

December 11, 1984

due to be released on parole on December 17. It is very difficult to understand why he committed this act when release was close at hand.
Finally, the security inquiry report is not yet complete. I look forward to receiving the report and the light it will shed on this particular case. I will, of course, share it with the Hon. Member, and I want to assure him that I take very seriously the other matters he has raised. I appreciate the need to
improve many of the factors which are still placing an undue burden on our system as far as the protection of Canadians is concerned.
